Wrapped Monero Token Collapses 99% After $13 Million Hack Blamed on Web Host

A wrapped version of Monero lost nearly all its value Friday after an attacker drained its deployer wallet and dumped the tokens on Hyperliquid.

XMR1, a token issued by cross-chain swap service Wagyu that represents Monero on Hyperliquid, fell more than 99% in roughly half an hour, from about $500 to around $1.

The account that deployed the token sent 5.2 million XMR1 to a newly created account early Friday, according to an analysis by onchain data firm Bitquery.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That account sold about 364,000 of the tokens to 388 buyers for $13.5 million, then converted the proceeds to ETH. At Bitquery’s last check, about 7,350 ETH sat in three wallets.

Wagyu’s pseudonymous founder, PerpetualCow, blamed a breach at 1984.hosting, an Icelandic web hosting provider.

He wrote on X that the XMR1 deployer key had been stored on an old server there that he had deleted, but that the host apparently kept its logs and files. “Lesson to learn here is that these hosting providers keep your data/logs even after you delete your server with them,” he wrote.

1984 ehf., the company behind the service, said it had suffered an extensive and serious cyberattack on its IT infrastructure, Icelandic outlet DV reported Friday, citing a joint statement with CERT-IS, Iceland’s national cybersecurity incident response team.

Early findings point to a well-organized and technically sophisticated attack, and the company said it couldn’t rule out that more systems were affected than it had confirmed. It temporarily shut down all services. The statement didn’t mention Wagyu or whether customer data was taken.

Turns out that the entire hosting provider of https://t.co/skXiWey4Fb got hacked with everyone's data + internal server files today.

The XMR1 deployer key was held on an OLD server on there that I DELETED, but…

— PerpetualCow.hl (@PerpetualCow) November 20, 2026

PerpetualCow said he would personally refund everyone who lost money and that Wagyu would relaunch later. “Give me some time please,” he wrote, but didn’t give a timeline.

Bitquery said onchain data alone can’t show whether the deployer’s key was stolen, and that it can’t see how much Monero backs the remaining XMR1, since the Monero side of the bridge isn’t visible.

The attacker’s account received its first funds from the crypto mixer Tornado Cash minutes before it was set up. The same deployer account still controls nearly all of ZEC1, a Zcash token. Wagyu also disclosed a separate data leak in October, saying at the time that funds were unaffected.

Wagyu surfaced earlier this month in ZachXBT’s tracing of a suspected $106 million theft from an unnamed European entity, in which part of the funds were converted to Monero through the service.

#5047. Fusionist ACE Bridge Exploit: $5.7M Loss Estimate, Bithumb Freezes Trading

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

The Fusionist ACE bridge exploit has produced an estimated $5.7 million in losses across two stages, according to SlowMist’s incident tracker. After unbacked ACE tokens were minted on BNB Chain and sold, traders reportedly used the resulting price collapse to withdraw real ACE from the project’s Endurance bridge reserves. The fallout reached centralized exchanges on Monday, November 23: Bithumb halted ACE trading after finding indications that abnormally issued tokens had entered crypto exchanges.

This was not one attacker walking away with $5.7 million in a single transaction. The distinction matters. Roughly $1.87 million was traced through the attacker’s proceeds, while another 53.7 million genuine ACE tokens, valued around $3.7 million at the incident’s reference prices, were reportedly withdrawn through the bridge. SlowMist lists a combined $5.7 million loss estimate, not an audited final total. The bridge’s most basic promise, that a token issued on one chain corresponds to something real on another, is precisely what now needs proving.

Security firm Blockaid flagged the Fusionist bridge-minter exploit on November 22. Its alert described the mechanism bluntly:

A privileged token-bridge minter minted unbacked ACE and sold it for USDT.

The firm initially estimated that about $1.04 million had been extracted while the attack was still ongoing. That was an interim snapshot, not a cap on the damage.

Blockchain-monitoring account Onchain Lens subsequently reported that an attacker had routed 1,091.5 ETH, valued at about $1.87 million at the time, through Tornado Cash. That observation traces a movement of proceeds, not an extra $1.87 million to add on top of the initial extraction estimate. The values describe different points in the same suspected attacker’s fund flow.

Fusionist acknowledged an apparent ongoing ACE exploit on BNB Smart Chain on Sunday and asked users to suspend transfers, trading and bridging on that network. It has not, in the material reviewed, provided a reconciled loss figure or a technical post-mortem identifying how the privileged minting authority was abused.

A bridge minter is supposed to create a token representation only when the corresponding value is properly accounted for. Once the right to mint is misused, a chain can show perfectly ordinary-looking balances that have no matching backing.

It is a familiar failure mode: NewsBTC previously covered a bridge-role exploit that minted unbacked tokens at CrediX. That earlier case does not establish Fusionist’s root cause, but it illustrates why elevated bridge permissions are such a consequential security boundary.

The subsequent drain may prove more important than the initial minting spree.

According to SlowMist’s November 22 incident entry, traders bought the sharply discounted ACE created by the market disruption and used the cross-chain bridge to withdraw about 53.7 million genuine ACE from the Endurance-side reserves. SlowMist valued that withdrawal at approximately $3.7 million.

Here is the mechanism without the jargon. A representation of ACE on BNB Chain suddenly became cheap because unauthorized supply had flooded the market. A bridge that would still accept those tokens in exchange for ACE on Endurance offered an obvious difference in value.

Anyone able to complete that conversion could receive real tokens in return for deeply discounted ones. The trading opportunity existed because the backing and the circulating representation were no longer in a trustworthy relationship.

The $3.7 million figure is a valuation of the ACE reserve outflow, not proof that every recipient sold those tokens for $3.7 million in cash. Nor does it mean every trader involved helped compromise the minter.

There is a meaningful difference between initiating the security breach and trading through a system whose defenses have already failed.

Those distinctions should not obscure the core problem. A bridge can have technically valid transactions and still produce an economically disastrous result. If unbacked supply can be redeemed for genuine reserves, the checks have failed where they matter most.

Bithumb suspended ACE deposits and withdrawals early on November 23. It then halted trading effective 7:30 a.m. Korea time, according to its follow-up ACE security notice.

The exchange said, in a translation from its Korean announcement, that it had:

confirmed indications that abnormally issued ACE had entered cryptocurrency exchanges.

It identified two related BNB Chain transactions and a second transaction.

Those records are important evidence leads, but a full independent decoding of the transaction trail remains outstanding.

Bithumb’s wording is careful: it reported signs of abnormal supply entering exchanges, not a finding that every ACE token in customer accounts is invalid. The trading suspension is a protective response, not a finalized determination of customer losses.

Still, it creates a practical problem for holders who never used the bridge. If tokens are fungible within a market, exchanges and the issuer need a credible method for identifying affected supply and deciding how deposits, balances and trades will be treated.

There is an understandable temptation to focus on the enormous minting figures. The more consequential question is what happened when those tokens met the bridge’s reserves.

A system does not need to lose control of its entire blockchain to suffer a serious failure in one privileged contract role. Nor should a successful-looking bridge transaction count as evidence that the asset being transferred was fully backed.

The response cannot end with a pause notice and a promise to investigate.

Fusionist needs to show which minting permissions were affected, whether they have been revoked, how much ACE was created without backing, how the Endurance-side reserve changed and what claims remain outstanding.

Exchanges need a defensible token-treatment plan, and holders need to know whether there is a shortfall and who is responsible for covering it.

There is a fair counterargument: the $5.7 million figure is an external estimate, market prices moved during the incident, and the precise compromise method is not established.

SlowMist categorizes the incident as private-key leakage, but that classification is not a substitute for an official technical finding. It would also be premature to treat a cautious exchange halt as proof that every affected customer suffered a loss.

Those qualifications change how the numbers should be reported. They do not make the underlying bridge-accounting failure less serious.

The next credible milestone is not a restored interface or a reassuring social post. It is a transparent reconciliation of the tokens minted, the reserves withdrawn and the assets still available to back legitimate ACE claims.

Until that exists, the estimated $5.7 million fallout remains a warning about both token security and the risks of trusting a bridge’s accounting.

#5043. Trump’s Meme Coin Dinner Exposes a 94% Collapse in Holder Commitments

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Donald Trump’s latest meme coin dinner came with a striking financial comparison: wallets displayed on the official $TRUMP dinner leaderboard held approximately $9.1 million in tokens at the November 16 cutoff, compared with roughly $148 million associated with the first dinner in May 2025. That puts the decline in the publicly measured dollar value at close to 94%. It does not mean investors withdrew 94% of their cash, or that 94% fewer people turned up for dinner.

Trump hosted the third event for major $TRUMP holders at his Virginia golf club on Sunday, November 22. The gathering itself was new, but the more interesting story is what the leaderboard reveals about a token that was once able to turn a private invitation into a market-wide buying contest. NewsBTC previously covered an earlier $TRUMP meme coin dinner rally. This time, the numbers tell a considerably less flattering story about the value attached to that privilege.

The roughly $9.1 million estimate comes from Public Citizen’s November 22 review of the 130 wallets displayed on the final public leaderboard. Its researchers counted 9,794,832.87 $TRUMP tokens and valued them at approximately $0.93 each at the November 16, 9 a.m. Eastern cutoff. The older $148 million comparison refers to the first gala’s leaderboard in May 2025.

Source: Official $TRUMP Gala Dinner Leaderboard (November 16, 2026). Rankings based on time-weighted token holdings. Wallet entries do not necessarily represent individual attendees.

That works out to a decline of roughly 93.9%, rounded to 94%. But the events did not have identical leaderboard sizes or necessarily identical valuation methods. More importantly, the token’s price fell dramatically between the two events. A lower marked-to-market balance can reflect falling prices even if some holders retain comparable token quantities.

Calling this a 94% collapse in new investment would therefore be wrong. The narrower conclusion is still hard to ignore: the value represented by the public competition for dinner access is a small fraction of what it was at the first event.

The leaderboard also should not be mistaken for a headcount. While the public display showed 130 wallets, organizers said 185 wallets qualified under the event’s rules. One person can control multiple wallets, and a wallet can be held for an organization. Neither figure identifies exactly who attended Sunday night’s dinner.

The smaller overall value is only part of the picture. Public Citizen found that the top 10 wallets held about 81% of the tokens on the public board. The top 29 accounted for approximately 95%. Those top-ranked wallets were also eligible for a special VIP reception.

The concentration matters because a leaderboard is marketed as a contest between investors, but its aggregate value can be dominated by a very small number of positions. Looking at the $9.1 million as if it represented broad, evenly distributed enthusiasm would be as misleading as treating all 130 wallet entries as separate people.

There is a revealing detail near the bottom of Public Citizen’s review: the wallet ranked No. 130 held only 9.71 $TRUMP, worth about $9 at the snapshot. It qualified because the competition measured time-weighted holdings over the scoring period, rather than the balance left in the wallet at the very end. That is perfectly compatible with the rules. It also shows why a dinner ranking cannot be read as a simple list of fresh purchases or long-term conviction.

There is another market point here. A buyer who wants dinner access can acquire the token and hedge some of the price risk elsewhere. Holding a spot position long enough to earn a place does not necessarily make someone a directional believer in the coin. In that sense, the competition measures an incentive to qualify, not a clean vote of confidence in future returns.

Public Citizen’s researchers traced 66 of the 130 displayed wallets, or 51%, to direct transfers from exchanges that restrict US customers. Those wallets represented about 4.35 million $TRUMP, roughly 44% of the public board’s token holdings. Among the top 29 VIP-ranked wallets, 15 had received tokens directly from such exchanges, according to the group’s November 22 findings.

That is useful on-chain information. It is not proof that 66 dinner guests were foreign nationals, that all those exchanges served prohibited customers, or that any particular attendee broke a rule. An exchange withdrawal identifies a source of tokens, not a passport or the identity of the person controlling the receiving wallet. Public Citizen put a basic transparency problem plainly: “The names of the invitees have not been disclosed.” That sentence matters because a wallet address, however transparent its transaction history, cannot supply the accountability that a named guest list would provide.

GetTrumpMemes.com is not political and has nothing to do with any political campaign or any political office or governmental agency.

That is the organizers’ characterization. It does not remove the transparency question created when holders of a president-linked digital asset can compete for personal access to the president. Neither does that question, by itself, prove an improper exchange of favors.

There is a credible bullish counterargument. An exclusive dinner is a limited, experience driven reward. Its value to attendees need not move in lockstep with the coin’s market capitalization, and falling token prices can make it cheaper for new participants to qualify. The gala went ahead, and its promoters continue to offer other experiences to holders.

But that is precisely why we should be careful about treating an invitation contest as evidence of a durable investment base. Access is an incentive. It is not a claim on business earnings, and it does not put a floor under the price of the coin.

The most uncomfortable part of this comparison for $TRUMP holders is not that the dinner was smaller or less glamorous. The available figures do not establish either claim. It is that the token’s most recognizable promotional feature remains personal access, while the dollar value visible on the public leaderboard has fallen dramatically since the first event.

In our view, that weakens the argument that repeated celebrity events, by themselves, can sustain the market’s appetite for the token. A more persuasive sign of recovering demand would be durable, independently observable holdings beyond a contest period, with less dependence on a few top-ranked wallets. The next useful data would be post-event wallet balances and exchange flows, measured against the November 16 snapshot, not just another photograph from the dinner.

For now, the 94% comparison is a warning about the dollar value of the visible leaderboard, not proof of a 94% investor exodus. That distinction makes the story more credible, and no less troubling for anyone relying on the dinner promotion as an investment thesis.

One rather unusual metric on XRP Ledger has seen more than a 3,062% increase in usage which raises a lot of questions. This is one of the largest spikes throughout the year in a function usage that mostly stays low.

The function allows users to manage their secondary keys for signing transactions on their wallets and/or accounts. Their main private keys stay offline, while a certain key issued by them is used in daily transactions.

It allows safer work and utilization of their wallets without potentially exposing their private keys. So even if someone grabs hold of your signing credentials, you'll be able to protect your funds by nullifying the issued keys, provided you still retain authorized access.

One way or another, the surge is bizarre. Most likely "legit" scenarios are: automated key rotations among large custodians like exchanges. Some security warnings that triggered massive migration and then, the illicit one: generation of function calls from bots or automated scripts.

The flatlined chart actually represents tens or hundreds of calls daily, but a surge to nearly 4,000 is certainly out of the blue. Unfortunately, we were unable to identify the source of those transactions.

The feature itself is legitimate, so the spike alone does not indicate that users' funds or wallets are at risk. However, an undisclosed exploit or security issue cannot be ruled out without further investigation.

One concerning scenario would involve malicious actors gaining access to wallets and assigning new regular keys to maintain control over them. This would not necessarily mean that the XRP Ledger itself has been compromised, but rather that individual accounts may have been targeted.

For now, there is no evidence pointing toward such an attack, and the activity could just as easily be attributed to routine security operations.

Still, XRP holders should keep an eye on any unexpected changes to their account settings, especially regular keys they did not authorize.

Whether this was a coordinated security upgrade, automated activity, or something more concerning remains unclear. What is certain is that such an unusual spike deserves closer attention, particularly if similar activity continues over the coming days.

#5041. Google Gives Gemini Control of Mac Apps, But Its New AI Agent Comes With Risks

Google Gives Gemini Control of Mac Apps, But Its New AI Agent Comes With Risks

Google wants Gemini to do more than answer questions on your Mac.

The company launched a computer-use feature Thursday that lets its AI assistant open applications, navigate menus, fill out forms, and move information between local files and websites on a user's behalf.

“Starting today, computer use in the Gemini app for Mac helps you get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” Google announced. “Just describe what you need, and Gemini handles the clicking, typing, menus, and forms for you.”

The new capability runs in what Google calls an isolated background window, leaving the computer's main display and cursor available for the owner. Users can watch the agent's actions through a live preview inside the Gemini chat and interrupt a task if it goes off course.

Google's examples include extracting shipping details from PDF documents and entering them into online forms, editing batches of photos, and building presentations from dashboard data. The company also suggests researching prices and preparing resale listings based on pictures stored on a Mac.

Those jobs involve a different kind of AI interaction than asking a chatbot to write instructions. Gemini is supposed to operate the software itself, carrying out the clicks and keystrokes that would otherwise fall to the user.

The feature is rolling out in English in the United States to adult users with personal paid Google accounts. It requires an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later; work and school accounts are not supported at launch.

To activate it, users enable computer use in the Mac app, open Task mode, and prompt Gemini with @Computer use. According to Google's support documentation, the assistant asks for permission before controlling a new app, with options to deny access, allow it once, or allow it on an ongoing basis.

Users can create lists of allowed and blocked apps, monitor the virtual screen, and stop a task. Google says sensitive actions require confirmation before the agent proceeds, though an app marked "always allow" can be accessed again without another app-level prompt.

Computer use adds a local dimension to Google's agent strategy. Decrypt previously covered Gemini Spark, the company's cloud-based task agent, while competitors have developed desktop-control tools including OpenAI's Codex, Anthropic's Claude, and Kimi Work.

The separate window is also a practical distinction: an agent that commandeers the visible cursor can make a computer difficult to use during a long task. Google's approach lets the person keep working while Gemini handles another workflow.

A background window should not be confused with a guarantee that files or accounts are isolated from risk. Google's own documentation warns that the agent can reach active sessions in desktop applications, encounter authentication codes displayed on screen, and take actions that some apps cannot reverse.

In that case, any error is the user’s fault, not Google’s.

It also warns about prompt injection, an attack in which malicious instructions hidden in a document or website persuade an AI system to do something its user never requested. With permission to operate multiple apps, Gemini could encounter hostile content in one program and act on it in another.

Google offers optional on-demand file backups but says they cannot always be created. Where they work, the temporary copies remain available for 24 hours or until the next prompt, and some applications may prevent their content from being backed up at all.

The launch also comes three days after Apple introduced tighter access controls in the macOS 27.3 beta. Those changes give users more ways to restrict powerful permissions to specific apps or folders and to require fresh approval each time access is requested.

Long-time Shiba Inu community member and SHIB developer, Mazrael, has reacted to Solana-based memecoin platform Pump.fun's recent wallet login changes, which are sparking concerns about private key security.

In a new announcement, Pump.fun stated that external wallet sign-in is being retired on November 30, 2026. Starting November 30, 2026 (15:00 UTC), Pump.fun on the web will only allow users to sign in with an email account or a Google, Apple, or GitHub account instead of an external wallet such as Phantom, Solflare, or Ledger.

Pump.fun reassures users that nothing will happen to their funds or account, as their wallet address, positions, callouts, followers and username remain unchanged. The only change is how users sign in.

Users who sign in to their accounts with Phantom or any other wallet are urged to take action before the November 30, 2026 deadline.

Pump.fun outlined a number of steps for users on how to switch their sign-in; of particular concern is the step that asked users to enter their wallet details and paste their private key when prompted. Pump.fun noted that this step encrypts the key in the user's browser and that the key is end-to-end encrypted by its login provider, Privy, allowing users' wallets to continue working for everything else.

Mazrael reacted to the development, drawing attention to the potential security implications for users.

pumpfun is retiring external wallet logins on web starting Nov 30. From then on you sign in with Google, Apple, email or GitHub. To keep your existing account..... they want you to paste your private key into their Privy flow 😬 Also note their own terms says they won’t ask for private keys...

The standard security practice across the cryptocurrency industry is that exchanges, wallet providers and other platforms do not ask users to disclose their private keys or recovery phrases. Such warnings are routinely issued to protect users from unauthorized access to their funds.

The Pump.fun wallet login change process appears to contradict this widely promoted security principle, Mazrael noted.

Private keys are highly sensitive credentials that give holders direct access to their cryptocurrency wallets. Whoever gets their hands on them might be able to access those wallets and move the funds. In general, it is recommended never to share private keys with individuals, support agents or third-party services.

#5038. Big XRP Holders Add $72 Million While Supply Hardens

Home » Ripple (XRP) » Big XRP Holders Add $72 Million While Supply Hardens

Big-time holders draw attention to XRP’s liquidity pockets sub-$1: is a bounce back signal getting delivered?

Large XRP holders have added roughly $72 million worth of tokens in recent days, even as major Bitcoin and Ethereum investors have reduced exposure during the broader market pullback.

The buying has coincided with a drop in available XRP on Binance, where reserves have reportedly fallen below levels last seen in July.

The move does not yet signal a clear bullish reversal. XRP was trading near $0.97, down about 3.6% over the previous week and still below its 200-day moving average near $1.26.

The combination of whale accumulation and thinner exchange balances has drawn attention to whether modest returning demand could produce a sharper price response.

An exchange supply-shortage measure for XRP rose to 2.4 on November 19, 2026 above its July reading of 2.09. Usually, readings above 2 are generally associated with unusually limited immediately available supply on the venue.

#XRP supply on Binance is getting tight. The Supply Shortage Index spiked above 8 in November and sits at 2.4 now, while price is still near $0.96.Supply is tightening and price has not responded yet. pic.twitter.com/xMTksTkKim

Large wallets also pulled more than $127 million in XRP from Binance on a net basis between November 10 and 16, 2026.

Some of those movements may reflect internal exchange reserve management rather than pure investor withdrawals, particularly after operational disruption at the platform, so the flows are not a definitive accumulation signal on their own.

Lower balances can still matter if spot demand returns. Fewer tokens sitting on exchanges may reduce readily available selling pressure, especially if a portion of the withdrawn XRP is moving into longer-term storage rather than being repositioned for immediate trading elsewhere.

US spot XRP ETFs have gone 15 consecutive trading days without a net inflow, their longest dry spell since launch. Since their last positive day on October 29, the funds have recorded net withdrawals of about $26.3 million.

Total XRP ETF assets have fallen to roughly $1.08 billion from $1.77 billion in late September, though cumulative inflows since launch remain close to $1.78 billion. Existing holders have not abandoned the products in large numbers, but fresh capital has paused.

The divergence is the central feature of the current setup: large holders have been willing to buy into weakness, while ETF demand has stayed on the sidelines.

Tighter exchange supply could amplify a recovery if broader buying returns, but without renewed fund inflows and a reclaim of key technical levels, scarcity alone is unlikely to reverse the trend.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

The hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts said last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, shows that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

According to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

The green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

The Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

Since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

The Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

Goldman also said that retail investors have been buying big tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

The Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

In the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

#5032. Solana Price Prediction 2030: Is $2,000 SOL Still on the Table After a 75% Crash?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Solana has lost roughly 75% of its value since reaching an all-time high of $294 in January 2025. Large futures traders are leaning bearish, yet institutional analysts continue to see a future in which SOL trades at four digit prices. So, how realistic is a $2,000 Solana price prediction for 2030?

At around $73, SOL is trading at a fraction of the price some of Wall Street’s most optimistic forecasts suggest it could eventually reach. But a steep discount to an analyst’s target does not necessarily make an asset cheap.

NewsBTC examined liquidation heatmaps, whale positions, historical price action, network economics and institutional valuation models to understand where Solana stands today and what it could realistically be worth by the end of the decade.

The findings paint a more complicated picture than either bulls or bears might expect.

Perhaps the most interesting signal right now comes from the derivatives market.

According to a November 23 snapshot from PumpGlass, only around 20% of the tracked Binance whale position value was allocated to longs. Meanwhile, approximately 79% of the broader trader accounts were positioned long.

Although the two figures measure different aspects of market positioning, the divergence is striking. Large traders appear considerably less optimistic than the wider trading crowd.

The average entry price of tracked whale shorts stood near $77.63, compared with $77.05 for whale longs. With SOL trading around $73 at the time of observation, the short side was better positioned.

The on-chain picture offers another reason for caution.

On November 19, blockchain tracker Lookonchain reported that two large holders had unstaked a combined 2.31 million SOL worth approximately $169.4 million before transferring the tokens to Coinbase Prime-associated addresses.

Exchange deposits do not necessarily mean those tokens were sold. Institutional investors use custody platforms for several purposes, including collateral management and portfolio rebalancing. Still, the movement is worth monitoring.

What matters now is whether large holders begin accumulating again or whether the recent decline has further to run.

Solana’s liquidation heatmap reveals an interesting battle developing around its current trading range.

PumpGlass identified several concentrations of potentially vulnerable leveraged positions in its November 23, 19:22 UTC observation.

A recovery toward $79 could put considerable pressure on short sellers. Conversely, a breakdown below $69 could expose another wave of leveraged longs to forced closures.

Data from CoinGlass adds another layer to the picture. At 21:31 UTC on November 23, Solana’s futures open interest stood at $3.86 billion, while rolling 24-hour liquidations reached approximately $30.59 million. Shorts accounted for roughly 72% of those liquidations.

SOL had gained around 3.1% over the same rolling period.

The recovery is consistent with some bearish positions being forced out of the market. However, a liquidated short is not the same as a new investor buying SOL for the next four years.

Until stronger spot demand emerges, traders should be careful about interpreting a short squeeze as the beginning of a sustainable recovery.

Liquidation concentrations are modeled estimates, not guaranteed future orders, and can change considerably as traders adjust their positions.

Solana’s price structure has deteriorated considerably since its September recovery.

After closing July near $72.79, SOL climbed to $103 in August and $117.99 in September. The recovery subsequently unraveled, with October closing near $95.35 before prices returned to the low $70s in November.

Looking at SOL’s historical price action on Binance, using the TradingView SOLUSDT market as the chart reference, five key price regions stand out:

The daily Relative Strength Index was in the low 30s in the observed CoinGlass data, suggesting weak momentum and proximity to oversold territory.

But oversold markets can remain oversold.

A sustained recovery above $80 would be the first encouraging development. Reclaiming $95 and subsequently $100 would provide stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control.

On the downside, failure to hold the $65 range would bring Solana’s 2026 low near $60.42 back into focus.

Our technical assessment remains cautious. There is room for a meaningful relief rally, particularly given the nearby short-liquidation exposure, but the broader market structure has yet to establish a convincing reversal.

While Solana’s price has struggled, its blockchain continues to facilitate substantial financial activity.

According to DefiLlama, Solana’s November 23 network metrics included:

There is something particularly interesting about those last two figures.

Applications running on Solana generated considerably more revenue than the chain itself under DefiLlama’s respective measurement definitions.

This highlights what could become Solana’s biggest valuation challenge.

A blockchain can attract substantial activity and billions of dollars in trading volume without its native token capturing a proportional share of that economic value.

Cheap transactions are excellent for adoption. Whether they are equally good for SOL’s valuation is another question entirely.

That is why Solana’s expansion beyond speculative trading could prove so important.

The blockchain’s growing presence in stablecoins, payments and tokenized real-world assets opens the door to financial activity that could persist even when speculative markets cool.

Its infrastructure is also evolving. The Solana Foundation reported the activation of Alpenglow in October 2026, targeting transaction finality near 150 milliseconds. November’s introduction of Solana 1.0 marked another milestone in the network’s development.

Meanwhile, the announced integration with DTCC’s Tokenization Service, expected in the second half of 2027, could represent a meaningful institutional opportunity.

The real test will be how much financial activity these developments ultimately bring onchain, and how much value SOL captures from it.

Institutional research offers a glimpse into how differently analysts view Solana’s future.

VanEck’s October 2023 research produced one of the widest forecast ranges, with its most optimistic scenario placing SOL above $3,200.

Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick was reported in February 2026 to have projected a $2,000 Solana price by 2030, partly based on the network’s potential in stablecoin micropayments.

However, the bank’s reported $250 end-of-2026 target looks increasingly difficult to achieve from current levels. Its original research note was not available for independent review.

Perhaps the most interesting analysis comes from Bitwise’s November 2026 research, which connects Solana’s future valuation to tokenized stock trading.

The asset manager’s base case assumes Solana captures 50% of tokenized-stock trading volume in 2031, generating approximately $6.75 billion in annual network economic value.

Applying a 40-times valuation multiple produces an estimated SOL price of $385, based on a projected total supply of 700 million tokens.

The report acknowledges the key dependency:

Most of the price increase depends on how quickly stocks move onchain.

In its bullish scenario, Solana captures 65% of tokenized-stock trading, generating approximately $12.83 billion in network economic value and supporting a modeled price of $1,100.

These assumptions reveal just how much needs to go right before four-digit SOL prices become fundamentally convincing.

Here is something many price predictions overlook: Solana’s token supply will not necessarily remain where it is today.

Unlike Bitcoin, SOL has no fixed maximum supply. Its inflationary issuance framework rewards validators and staking participants, while future governance decisions can influence the rate of supply growth.

With around 592 million SOL currently circulating, we use an illustrative assumption of 690 million total tokens by 2030 for our valuation scenarios.

The numbers put popular price targets into perspective.

These are total-supply valuations rather than projected circulating market capitalizations.

At $2,000, Solana would need to command a valuation of approximately $1.38 trillion under our assumptions.

Using Bitwise’s base-case valuation multiple of 40 times annual network economic value as an illustrative benchmark, Solana would need to generate approximately $34.5 billion in annual economic value to support that figure.

Even at a more generous 60-times multiple, the requirement would be $23 billion annually.

That is substantially more demanding than simply attracting another wave of cryptocurrency traders.

Based on the network’s economic opportunity, competitive landscape, token supply and institutional research, NewsBTC has developed four conditional valuation scenarios.

These ranges are conditional editorial scenarios, not statistically derived forecasts. Outcomes outside these ranges, including substantially greater losses, are possible.

Solana remains relevant but struggles to turn network adoption into meaningful economic value for SOL. Institutional projects develop more slowly than expected, competitors gain market share, and speculative trading remains an important source of demand.

Solana does not need to fail for this scenario to materialize. It only needs to fall short of the expectations investors have placed on it.

Our central expectation assumes Solana retains its position among the leading smart-contract networks while expanding its role in payments, DeFi and tokenized financial assets.

Under this scenario, the network does not need to dominate global finance. It needs to establish a durable position within it and capture more economic value from the applications it supports.

Solana becomes a major platform for tokenized equities, stablecoin settlements and high-frequency financial applications.

Institutional adoption moves beyond announcements, network revenue expands significantly, and the broader cryptocurrency market benefits from favorable liquidity conditions.

At $1,000, SOL would trade at approximately 13.8 times its November 23 reference price.

This is where the most ambitious institutional predictions become conceivable.

Solana would need to capture a significant share of a much larger on-chain financial economy, scale its infrastructure accordingly, and translate that activity into sustained demand for SOL.

An exceptional cryptocurrency bull market could also temporarily push valuations beyond what underlying economics justify.

We would not consider this the most likely outcome based on today’s evidence.

Rather than following every new price target, long-term SOL investors may benefit from monitoring five developments:

Competition from Ethereum, its scaling ecosystem and specialized financial networks remains a considerable risk.

If Solana’s transaction volumes rise while the economic value captured by the network stagnates, we would have reason to lower our valuation assumptions, regardless of how impressive the adoption statistics look.

The current market offers an interesting contradiction.

Solana’s blockchain has established a meaningful financial ecosystem, yet its token is trading roughly 75% below its historical record. Large futures traders are cautious, while institutional research continues to outline substantial long-term opportunities.

Our $180 to $400 base-case range for 2030 reflects the possibility that Solana can grow without fulfilling every ambitious expectation placed on it.

A move toward $1,000 is conceivable under considerably stronger conditions. At $2,000, however, investors would be betting on Solana becoming one of the world’s most valuable digital financial networks.

The opportunity is there. The evidence that would justify such a valuation is not there yet.

For now, the most interesting question surrounding Solana is not how many transactions it can process, but how much those transactions will eventually be worth to SOL holders.

NewsBTC’s analysis places Solana between $180 and $400 by 2030 under our base-case scenario. Strong institutional adoption and improved network economics could support a bullish range of $600 to $1,000, while weaker growth could leave SOL trading between $40 and $110.

Solana could reach $500 by 2030 if its adoption across payments, DeFi and tokenized financial assets continues to expand. Based on an assumed total supply of 690 million SOL, a $500 price would imply a total-supply valuation of approximately $345 billion.

A $1,000 Solana price is possible under a strong bullish scenario. However, achieving and sustaining that valuation would require substantial institutional adoption, higher network economic value and favorable cryptocurrency market conditions. At $1,000, Solana’s implied total-supply valuation would reach approximately $690 billion.

Standard Chartered was reported to have projected a $2,000 SOL price by 2030 in February 2026. However, our analysis considers this an extreme bullish scenario. Reaching $2,000 would imply a total-supply valuation of approximately $1.38 trillion, requiring extraordinary growth in Solana’s financial ecosystem and demand for SOL.

While mathematically possible, a $10,000 SOL price would imply a valuation of approximately $6.9 trillion based on our 2030 supply assumption. There is currently insufficient economic evidence to support such a valuation within this timeframe.

Solana offers long-term exposure to decentralized finance, stablecoin payments and institutional asset tokenization. However, its investment potential depends on whether growing network adoption translates into sustainable demand for SOL. Competition, token inflation, market volatility and regulatory developments remain significant risks.

Solana could challenge Ethereum in areas such as decentralized trading, payments and financial applications. However, overtaking Ethereum by market capitalization would require substantial growth in Solana’s economic value, institutional demand and developer ecosystem. Higher transaction volumes alone would not guarantee that outcome.

VanEck’s October 2023 research placed SOL at $334.70 in its base case and $3,211.28 in its most optimistic scenario for 2030. Standard Chartered was reported to have projected $2,000 in February 2026, while Bitwise’s November 2026 research estimated a base-case price of $385 and a bullish price of $1,100 for 2031.

Weak spot demand, large-holder selling, leveraged liquidations, network disruptions and deteriorating global liquidity could all contribute to further declines. From a technical perspective, losing the $60 to $65 support region identified in our November 23, 2026 analysis would significantly weaken the recovery outlook.

Using the November 23, 2026 reference price of $72.52, a $1,000 investment would purchase approximately 13.79 SOL.

These hypothetical calculations exclude staking rewards, trading fees and taxes. Actual returns may differ substantially, and investors could lose their entire investment.

This analysis uses CoinGlass and PumpGlass market observations dated November 23, 2026, at 21:31 UTC and 19:22 UTC, respectively. Network metrics are provisional DefiLlama observations dated November 23. Technical analysis uses historical Binance SOLUSDT candles. NewsBTC’s valuation scenarios assume 690 million total SOL in 2030 and are conditional editorial estimates rather than statistical forecasts. Third-party forecasts retain their original publication dates and time horizons. Cryptocurrency investments involve significant risk, including loss of principal.

#5031. XRP’s Below $1 Not For Long? Supply Tightens

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP’s Below $1 Not For Long? Supply Tightens

XRP has slipped below the $1 mark even as the amount available on Binance is tightening sharply.

XRP has fallen below the $1 level even as available supply on Binance appears to be shrinking, leaving the token between constrained exchange inventory and a lack of fresh institutional buying.

Recent reports put XRP near $0.95 after a steep monthly decline, with the token briefly trading under $0.90 during November’s broader sell-off. Intermittent rebounds have occurred, but price has not yet established a durable hold above the $1 mark.

US spot XRP ETFs have gone through their longest stretch without a net inflow since launch, according to SoSoValue data. The funds last recorded an $8.43 million net inflow on October 29 and have since seen roughly $26 million in withdrawals, though flows on November 18 and 19 were described as flat rather than net negative.

The pause matters because ETF buyers had previously provided incremental demand. Total net assets in the funds stood at about $1.08 billion by November 19, down from roughly $1.77 billion in late September, while cumulative inflows since launch remained near $1.8 billion.

XRP’s price action reflects that gap. The token was down about 3.6% over one recent seven-day period and roughly 28% over the prior month in another snapshot. Its 30-day Sharpe ratio was reported near negative 0.41, indicating that recent returns have not compensated for the asset’s volatility.

CryptoQuant’s XRP Supply Shortage Index for Binance rose to 2.4 on November 19, above its July reading of 2.09. Readings above 2 are described as severe tightness, and net withdrawals from the exchange exceeded $127 million between November 10 and 16.

Lower exchange balances can reduce immediately available selling inventory, but they do not form a standalone bullish signal. One analyst noted that part of the movement could reflect internal Binance reserve management rather than accumulation by long-term holders.

XRP’s price action has not yet confirmed stronger demand. XRP remains below its 200-day moving average, sitting very near $1.26, and repeated closes below $1 have turned that former support into nearby resistance.

Traders are watching the $0.94 area first, followed by support around $0.88. A sustained break below the latter could open a path toward $0.80, while a recovery would need to reclaim roughly $0.985 and then $1 before a broader reversal appears more credible.

The more relevant signal for the market is whether ETF flows resume as Bitcoin and broader risk sentiment stabilize. Tighter supply can amplify a move higher, but without returning demand it can also coexist with a fragile price floor.

#5028. SBF’s 'The Altruists' Plot Twist: FTX’s Anthropic Shares Would Be Worth $43 Billion

SBF’s 'The Altruists' Plot Twist: FTX’s Anthropic Shares Would Be Worth $43 Billion

Sam Bankman-Fried had an eventful Thursday—at least on the internet.

Anthropic went public, Netflix released “The Altruists,” and Crypto Twitter imagined the fortune his collapsed exchange might have made by keeping its AI investment.

At Anthropic’s November 19 closing price of $97.17, FTX’s former shares would have been worth $43.28 billion. At the $111.50 opening trade, their theoretical value would have reached $49.66 billion.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That money never belonged personally to Bankman-Fried. The bankruptcy estate sold the shares to repay creditors after FTX’s 2022 collapse.

The former CEO is serving a 25-year sentence for fraud after using FTX customer funds to make investments and cover losses, plus got hit with $11 billion in forfeiture—a fraction of what his single Anthropic investment would have returned today.

A company linked to Alameda, FTX’s sister company, committed $500 million to Anthropic in October 2021. The money converted into roughly 44.54 million preferred shares during the AI startup’s 2022 Series B, about 13.6% of the company.

Bankruptcy administrators sold the position in two batches in 2024 for approximately $1.34 billion. Buyers included an Abu Dhabi-linked fund and Jane Street, Bankman-Fried’s former employer, as filings showed.

At Thursday’s closing price that investment would have produced a total of nearly $43.28 billion—roughly 32 times what creditors’ administrators actually collected.

Sadly, that fortune is hypothetical. Later financing diluted FTX’s percentage ownership, the shares carried restrictions, and the estate needed liquidity to compensate customers who lost money when FTX went belly up. A judge approved the sale in February 2024.

Tiffany Fong, who rose to Twitter fame after interviewing SBF just before he was arrested, shared an AI-generated video of a crying Bankman-Fried drinking in a car alongside the $40 billion-plus calculation. Another account posted a crying-man meme about him watching the listing from prison.

Sam Bankman-Fried’s $500 million investment in Anthropic would now be worth over $40 billion.

The FTX estate sold it for only $1.34 billion during bankruptcy. pic.twitter.com/H2tua0D4V0

— Tiffany Fong (@TiffanyFong) November 20, 2026

Vietnamese commentator Yuki Sato likened the predicament to selling a house to settle debts before its value increased 100-fold. French poster Mehdi lamented SBF’s short-time focus.

FTX creditor advocate Sunil Kavuri reminded followers that customer deposits had funded the original investment and that the estate sold it to repay customers. Separate Anthropic investments tied to Caroline Ellison and Nishad Singh were handled through government forfeiture, so not the same estate sale, but still related in Crypto Twitter’s collective mind.

FTX customers funds used to invest in Series B at $2.5bn valuation

SBF invested $500m in Anthropic using FTX customer deposits in Series B (Valuation: $2.5bn)7.8% stake was sold for $1.3bn in 2024

Nishad Singh ($40m) and Caroline Ellison ($10m)…

— Sunil (FTX Creditor Champion) (@sunil_trades) November 19, 2026

FTX and Alameda’s portfolio extended far beyond Anthropic. A leaked investment spreadsheet showed roughly $5.4 billion allocated to around 500 bets. These are some of the most important ones:

Alameda put $200,000 into Anysphere, maker of the AI coding tool. The estate sold the stake for the same amount in 2023. SpaceX acquired the company at a $60 billion valuation in 2026. If the original holding was about 5%, its undiluted value would be near $3 billion; subsequent dilution makes that an upper-bound mark.

The estate sold roughly 25 million to 30 million locked SOL tokens near $64 each in 2024, Bloomberg reported. At SOL’s January 2025 high of $293.31, that tranche would have been worth a bit less than $9 billion.

Bankman-Fried’s vehicle spent about $648 million on Robinhood shares in 2022. Authorities seized 55.27 million shares, which Robinhood repurchased for $605.7 million in 2023. At the stock’s 2025 intraday high of $153.86, that block would have been worth approximately $8.5 billion.

Alameda’s $1.15 billion Genesis Digital investment would imply around $290 million at a 2026 transaction valuation. By contrast, $40 million in drone maker BRINC could mark near $109 million at a funding estimate, and $20 million in Anchorage Digital about $31 million at its 2026 valuation.

A 461-position reconstruction puts $5.32 billion in total investments at roughly $59.5 billion on today’s valuation for those companies and assets—about $54.2 billion in hypothetical gains. The model assumes all investments were held and imputes values for illiquid positions.

That’s good for a 1,018% return, and proof SBF knew how to pick his bets. But even the best investments can't justify gambling with other people's money without their consent. He made that bet, too—and lost.

#5026. Bitcoin Reserves Just Found a New Use on Wall Street, but There’s a Catch

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Bitcoin reserves have found another potential use within the US financial system. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has clarified that regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses can count Bitcoin, Ethereum and qualifying payment stablecoins toward certain financial resource requirements. However, the regulator is not prepared to treat those holdings like cash.

The guidance, issued on November 23, could give regulated trading venues greater flexibility in managing their balance sheets. For Bitcoin investors, however, the more interesting question is whether that flexibility will translate into fresh institutional demand.

The answer is not quite as straightforward as it might seem.

The CFTC’s latest advisory addresses three types of regulated businesses: swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organizations.

These institutions are required to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover at least one year of operating costs. Under the new staff guidance, Bitcoin, Ether and qualifying payment stablecoins may contribute toward those requirements, subject to appropriate valuation discounts.

The announcement follows broader efforts to integrate digital assets into regulated financial infrastructure. NewsBTC previously reported on the CFTC’s guidance concerning tokenized collateral at clearinghouses, another area where traditional financial markets are gradually accommodating blockchain-based assets.

This time, the discussion is not about what traders can post as collateral. It is about the assets that the institutions running those markets can rely on to keep their businesses operating.

For a company that already holds Bitcoin, the clarification could make those holdings more useful from a regulatory standpoint. For businesses considering adding cryptocurrency to their balance sheets, it removes some uncertainty surrounding how those assets would be recognized.

But that recognition comes at a discount!

The CFTC advisory references a minimum 20% valuation haircut for Bitcoin and Ethereum, consistent with earlier staff treatment of proprietary cryptocurrency positions held by futures commission merchants.

Qualifying payment stablecoins receive considerably more favorable treatment, with a referenced haircut of 2%.

An exchange holding $10 million in Bitcoin, for example, would be able to count $8 million toward the relevant financial resource requirement if it applied a 20% haircut and no further deductions were necessary.

The remaining $2 million is not a realized loss. It is a regulatory adjustment intended to account for the risk associated with holding a volatile asset.

Crypto assets that are neither readily marketable nor qualifying payment stablecoins would generally face a 100% haircut, effectively excluding them from the calculation.

Perhaps the most revealing part of the advisory is the regulator’s warning about what it calls wrong-way risk.

A DCM should consider potential wrong-way risk

For a cryptocurrency-focused exchange, that risk is particularly relevant. A prolonged Bitcoin sell-off could put pressure on trading revenues while simultaneously reducing the value of the assets the exchange relies on to support its operations.

The problem is not simply that Bitcoin is volatile. It is that its value could deteriorate at precisely the moment a crypto business finds itself under financial pressure.

A 20% valuation discount provides some protection against that scenario, but it is hardly a guarantee.

Despite allowing digital assets to contribute toward broader operating resources, the CFTC has maintained a separate requirement for cash and highly liquid securities.

Bitcoin, Ethereum and even qualifying payment stablecoins cannot be used to satisfy that particular obligation under the advisory.

Swap execution facilities must maintain qualifying liquid resources sufficient to cover at least three months of projected operating expenses or the cost of winding down their operations, whichever is greater.

For designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organizations, the operating-cost liquidity requirement generally covers at least six months.

The distinction matters because an institution can have substantial assets on its balance sheet without necessarily having the cash available to meet immediate obligations.

It is also worth noting that the guidance does not address whether cryptocurrencies can satisfy the separate financial resources that clearinghouses must maintain to cover clearing-member defaults.

In effect, the CFTC is recognizing Bitcoin as an asset that can contribute to an institution’s financial strength without giving it the same regulatory standing as cash.

That is a more cautious approach than some Bitcoin advocates might have hoped for, but arguably a more sustainable one for integrating cryptocurrency into financial infrastructure.

The bullish interpretation is relatively simple. If regulated financial institutions can derive greater utility from holding Bitcoin, more of them may eventually consider allocating capital to the cryptocurrency.

The expansion of regulated crypto infrastructure has already brought digital assets closer to traditional financial markets. Earlier, NewsBTC reported on Coinbase’s CFTC registration for its USDC-focused derivatives clearinghouse, illustrating how cryptocurrency businesses are increasingly operating within established regulatory frameworks.

The latest advisory gives relevant institutions another reason to evaluate how digital assets fit into their balance sheets.

Still, there is a considerable difference between allowing an institution to hold Bitcoin for regulatory purposes and giving it an economic incentive to buy more.

An exchange that already owns Bitcoin could benefit from the clarification without purchasing a single additional coin. Another might conclude that holding conventional securities remains more efficient, particularly given the valuation discounts and separate liquidity requirements.

Nothing in the advisory requires institutions to acquire Bitcoin, and no purchase commitments were disclosed alongside the announcement.

Investors should therefore resist the temptation to translate this development directly into a bullish price forecast.

The longer-term significance may be greater than the immediate market impact. Every additional recognized use for Bitcoin within regulated financial markets strengthens the case for its utility beyond speculative trading.

However, the November 23 document remains a staff advisory rather than a binding rule adopted by the full Commission. It does not amend existing regulations or create enforceable rights.

The next meaningful development will be evidence that regulated institutions are actually changing their reserve allocations in response.

Until then, Bitcoin has gained another form of regulatory recognition. Whether it gains another source of sustained buying pressure is a different question entirely.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the SEC was investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors. Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, said the inquiry centers on potential accounting issues, though it couldn’t confirm when the probe began or exactly what the agency is examining.

The SEC declined to comment, and Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to Reuters. Investigations aren’t evidence of wrongdoing, and many close without enforcement action.

Renewed attention has fallen on a change Nvidia made last year to how it reports revenue by geography. It switched from customers’ billing addresses to their headquarters, which removed Singapore from its regional breakdown.

The Financial Times reported this week that Nvidia made the switch as Singapore sales climbed to nearly half its global revenue. Reuters didn’t say whether the change is part of the SEC’s inquiry.

Investors have also grown wary of circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers help customers fund chip purchases and data center construction. On Tuesday’s earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said Nvidia would be far more selective about such financing going forward.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week following reports of extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang.

Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, and U.S. authorities suspect her of being a Chinese spy; China has denied she is a spy.

U.S. authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible export control violations tied to alleged shipments of Nvidia chips to China, according to the Justice and Commerce departments.

Former CEO Huang said Tuesday he would be honored to return if the board believed it would benefit shareholders and employees. Hours later, the board shut that down.

“The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call, adding that the company had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.

The crisis has erased more than a third of Nvidia’s market value, even after the company beat expectations Tuesday with $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% from a year earlier.

Crypto exchange Kraken recently faced a flash crash that was caused by a liquidity shortage in one of its Canadian-dollar trading markets, rather than an actual crash in Bitcoin [BTC]’s global market price.

Over the weekend, Bitcoin’s price on Kraken’s BTC/CAD trading pair suddenly dropped to C$24,250. This was equivalent to approximately $16,900 at the prevailing USD/CAD exchange rate.

This came as a shock because Bitcoin was trading around $57,650 on Kraken’s BTC/USD market during that period. In Bitcoin trading at nearly 70% below its price on other markets.

However, this was not a market-wide Bitcoin crash, as other major exchanges continued to show Bitcoin trading between $55,000 and $60,000.

The primary suspected reason was a sudden shortage of liquidity in Kraken’s BTC/CAD order book. This liquidity shortage, aka liquidity vacuum, is what caused a sudden price crash without Bitcoin’s actual market value declining.

Expressing their opinion on the matter, Blockstream CEO Adam Back suggested that the disruption may have originated from a market maker running out of funds in Kraken’s USD/CAD market.

As expected, this distortion may have spread to other CAD trading pairs through arbitrage, where traders buy assets at lower prices and sell them elsewhere at higher prices.

However, Kraken has not confirmed this explanation, yet. The exchange maintained that all orders were processed correctly and refused to reverse completed trades.

This followed the exchange experiencing a one-hour technical outage on 30 October 2026, affecting its website, app, and trading APIs.

But at the same time, Kraken recently expanded its xStocks platform to over 1,000 tokenized stock listings, according to AMBCrypto’s previous report.

#5020. Binance Hack: US Moves to Recover $1.1 Billion, but Who Gets the Money?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Nearly four weeks after the Binance hack, US authorities have filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the October theft. The money is already subject to restrictions, but the latest court filings reveal a complication: freezing stolen cryptocurrency is considerably easier than returning it.

The complaint, filed on November 23, in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, targets USDC associated with 36 cryptocurrency addresses across 18 blockchains.

Federal investigators attribute the October 29 attack to North Korean hacking groups, including the Lazarus Group. The complaint puts the value of the original theft at approximately $6 billion.

For Binance, the latest legal action represents another opportunity to recover a portion of its losses. For the wider cryptocurrency industry, however, the case raises questions about the authority stablecoin issuers exercise over digital assets and what happens when governments become involved.

The assets targeted by US authorities are not an entirely new discovery.

Earlier this month, NewsBTC reported that Circle had frozen approximately $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the Binance hack, following cooperation with law enforcement.

What has changed is the government’s attempt to establish a legal basis for taking possession of those assets.

According to the court documents, US authorities obtained a temporary restraining order on November 12. Prosecutors subsequently requested that the restrictions remain in place throughout the civil forfeiture proceedings.

Both Binance and Circle consented to the initial restraining order and the requested extension, according to the government’s November 23 application.

The agreement between the companies and federal authorities reduces one immediate obstacle to preserving the funds. It does not, however, resolve the question of their ultimate ownership or distribution.

Civil forfeiture proceedings are directed against property believed to be connected to criminal activity. Interested parties can assert legitimate claims to that property through the legal process.

In this case, prosecutors are seeking forfeiture of the assets to the United States. That is not the same thing as a court ordering their immediate return to Binance.

Perhaps the most interesting disclosure in the complaint concerns Circle itself.

The stablecoin issuer can restrict transfers involving USDC held at particular blockchain addresses. However, that authority does not necessarily give Circle direct control over the wallets holding those tokens.

does not have the technical ability to transfer the Defendant Property from the blocklisted Subject Addresses to the United States

Instead, Circle has agreed to issue an equivalent amount of replacement USDC and transfer those tokens to US authorities upon receiving a forfeiture order from the court.

The proposed arrangement exposes an unusual feature of centralized stablecoins. An issuer can prevent tokens from circulating without possessing the private keys needed to move them.

It also raises an accounting question that deserves attention. If replacement tokens are issued, what ultimately happens to the original frozen USDC, and how will Circle ensure that the treatment of those balances is reflected accurately in its outstanding supply and reserve reporting?

The issuance of replacement tokens would not, by itself, prove that USDC had become undercollateralized. Nevertheless, transparency around the implementation would be important for a stablecoin whose credibility depends on confidence in its backing.

The immediate concern is not whether Circle can create new tokens. It is whether the entire recovery process can be independently accounted for.

The temptation to describe the Justice Department’s announcement as a billion-dollar recovery is understandable. It is also premature.

There are three separate stages involved: restricting access to the stolen assets, obtaining legal authority over them and determining how they will ultimately be distributed.

The November 23 filings advance the second stage. They do not establish that the third has been completed.

There is also a cross-border complication.

On November 18, Reuters reported that an Abu Dhabi court had directed several cryptocurrency companies, including Circle, to preserve digital assets associated with the Binance theft.

The involvement of authorities in both the United States and the United Arab Emirates illustrates how a single cryptocurrency theft can generate legal proceedings across multiple jurisdictions.

Blockchain transactions may cross national borders without much difficulty. Establishing ownership rights over the assets involved is a considerably less straightforward exercise.

That does not mean the US and UAE proceedings are necessarily in conflict. But the ultimate disposition of the funds will require more than an announcement from either government.

For investors assessing Binance’s financial position, the distinction between frozen assets and recovered capital is particularly important. Restricted cryptocurrency should not automatically be treated as money already returned to the exchange.

For years, the ability of stablecoin issuers to freeze tokens has been criticized by advocates of decentralized finance.

The Binance case demonstrates the other side of that argument.

Without Circle’s ability to restrict transactions, preserving such a large amount of cryptocurrency for potential recovery would have been more difficult.

In this particular case, centralized control has provided a mechanism that may help prevent suspected criminals from benefiting from stolen assets.

The uncomfortable question is whether the cryptocurrency industry can benefit from that authority while also demanding meaningful safeguards against its misuse.

The answer depends partly on transparency. Token holders should be able to understand why assets were frozen, under what legal authority restrictions remain in place and how disputes over ownership are resolved.

The same standard should apply to the exchange, the stablecoin issuer and the government.

The next significant development in the Binance case will be the court’s treatment of the forfeiture claim and any competing claims to the assets. Circle’s proposed issuance of replacement USDC will also deserve scrutiny if it proceeds.

Until then, the $1.1 billion should be understood as assets subject to an ongoing recovery effort, not a completed repayment.

For a cryptocurrency industry that frequently celebrates the speed of moving money, the Binance hack is a reminder that getting it back can be an entirely different business.

#5018. Claude Claims Historic Math Breakthrough One Day After Anthropic IPO

Claude Claims Historic Math Breakthrough One Day After Anthropic IPO

An Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped him crack the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old puzzle with a $1 million prize attached.

His claim surfaced Friday, one day after the AI company’s stock-market debut, and has not yet been independently verified.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Levent Alpöge wrote in a four-page note. He says the method also resolves the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which extends the question to other mathematical functions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Alpöge says he and Claude encoded their argument in Lean, software used to check mathematical proofs step by step. His note links to 14 downloadable parts of the proof archive, but its availability does not amount to acceptance by the mathematical community.

Alpöge says he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about a possible announcement “late Sunday night,” November 15. He then consulted company leadership and said there was a constraint to respect, without explaining precisely what it was.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he acknowledged. Alpöge rejected a cynical interpretation of the timing, but did not explicitly say the company’s IPO caused the delay.

Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday, November 19, after raising $81.34 billion in its offering.

Alpöge figured in September’s AI math wars. OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem as he and NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster pursued related fluid-equation work, sparking a credit dispute over research priority.

OpenAI followed in October with 722 manuscripts generated by an unreleased model, grouped into 372 families of results. Only 162 included Lean-checked main results, and mathematicians demanded stronger evidence rather than accepting the company’s flood of claims at face value.

Some mathematicians fear a “mathocalypse,” with AI solving coveted problems before researchers can learn from pursuing them. Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt warned that, without adaptation, “there’s just no more math in 50 years.” At an MIT panel this week, Buckmaster argued mathematics still requires human understanding.

First posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis predicts where certain zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall. The question matters because those zeros are linked to the distribution of prime numbers, whose patterns underlie extensive mathematical research.

A proof would be a historic mathematical result, since experts have been trying to solve that for over a century.

Lean can verify that formal deductions obey its rules. Mathematicians still need to reproduce the archive, check the formalized theorem matches the original conjecture, and examine the claimed result before considering it settled.

Anthropic previously reported progress on the zeta function without claiming to solve the full hypothesis. Alpöge’s new assertion goes far beyond that earlier work.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the Riemann hypothesis among its Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million award. Under the institute’s prize rules, a proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, survive at least two years of scrutiny, and earn general acceptance before the prize can be considered.
